question.prompt:
From a regular octagon, a triangle is formed by connecting three randomly chosen vertices of the octagon. What is the probability that at least one of the sides of the triangle is also a side of the octagon?

[Figure 1](figures/2018_AMC_8_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Count triangles by first choosing an octagon side that belongs to the triangle. There are \(8\) sides, and after choosing its two endpoints, there are \(6\) possible third vertices. This gives \(8\cdot6=48\) counts.

Some triangles are counted twice: any three consecutive octagon vertices form a triangle containing two octagon sides. There are \(8\) such triangles, one centered at each vertex, and each was counted once for each of its two octagon sides. No triangle contains three octagon sides, since three sides of an octagon do not close into a triangle. Thus subtracting one extra count for each gives \(48-8=40\) favorable triangles.

The total number of three-vertex selections is

\[
\frac{8\cdot7\cdot6}{3\cdot2\cdot1}=56,
\]

where division removes the six orders of choosing the same three vertices. The probability is

\[
\frac{40}{56}=\boxed{\frac57},
\]

choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\). When counting by a triangle's sides, check whether a triangle can qualify through more than one side.
solutions.title: Count qualifying side incidences and remove double counts
